title: Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down)

meta.title: Who originally recorded "Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down)"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Nancy Sinatra. Cher recorded it first, on 11 February 1966, released by Imperial that month. Sonny Bono wrote it; Kill Bill made the cover famous.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down)'?
meta.ogDescription: Cher cut it first in February 1966 for Imperial, written by Sonny Bono. Nancy Sinatra's 1966 cover became the famous one via Kill Bill.

answer.label: Not a Nancy Sinatra original — a 1966 Cher single on Imperial
answer.sourceLine: Because Quentin Tarantino hung Nancy Sinatra’s reading over the opening credits of Kill Bill: Volume 1, a lot of people met the song as hers. It was Cher’s first: she cut it at Gold Star Studios in Los Angeles on 11 February 1966, and Imperial Records issued it as a single on 25 February 1966. It was written by Sonny Bono, then her husband. Far from being an obscure original, Cher’s record went to No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became her first million-selling single — the eclipse happened decades later, in a cinema.

original.released: Recorded 11 February 1966 at Gold Star Studios in Los Angeles and released as a single by Imperial Records on 25 February 1966. It also appeared on Cher’s second solo album, The Sonny Side of Chér.
original.charted: A major hit — No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 3 on the UK Singles Chart. It was Cher’s first million-selling single.
original.cover: Nancy Sinatra’s version, arranged by Billy Strange, was a track on her Reprise album How Does That Grab You? (May 1966). It had no Hot 100 run of its own; its fame dates from 2003, when Quentin Tarantino placed it over the opening credits of Kill Bill: Volume 1.

trail: Wikipedia’s article on the song ↗ gives the recording date of 11 February 1966 at Gold Star Studios, the Imperial single release on 25 February 1966, and Cher’s peaks of No. 2 in the US and No. 3 in the UK.
MusicBrainz ↗ holds the Cher recording at 2:45, the length that matches the officially distributed 1966 single audio.
The Wikipedia entry for How Does That Grab You? ↗ places Nancy Sinatra’s version as a track on a Reprise album issued in May 1966 — after Cher’s single was already on the charts.
Songfacts ↗ confirms Sonny Bono’s authorship and records Sinatra’s own account of the Kill Bill revival.

authors.name: Cher
authors.heading: Cher
authors.metaLine: b. 1946 · American singer and actress · Imperial Records, 1966
authors.bio: Cherilyn Sarkisian was already half of Sonny & Chér when she recorded this on her own in February 1966, at the age of nineteen. The single was her breakthrough as a solo artist — No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 3 in the UK, and the first record of hers to sell a million. It appeared on her second solo album, The Sonny Side of Chér ↗.

authors.name: Nancy Sinatra
authors.heading: Nancy Sinatra
authors.bio: Sinatra recorded the song the same year for her Reprise album How Does That Grab You? ↗, arranged by Billy Strange, whose tremolo guitar figure is the version’s signature. It is a genuinely great record and the reason the song has a second life: Quentin Tarantino placed it over the opening credits of Kill Bill: Volume 1 in 2003. Sinatra herself credited the revival to “the lonely sound” of Strange’s guitar. The only error is chronological — hers is the cover.

authors.name: Sonny Bono
authors.heading: Sonny Bono
authors.metaLine: 1935–1998 · American songwriter, producer and later politician
authors.bio: Bono wrote the song and produced Cher’s recording of it. He and Cher were married at the time, and the Sonny & Cher partnership — his songs, her voice — produced most of her mid-1960s hits. He later left music for politics, serving as mayor of Palm Springs and then in the US House of Representatives.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The Nancy Sinatra recording is the one most people have heard, and it is easy to assume the famous version is the first one. It is not.

items.why: Her version, arranged by Billy Strange, appeared on the Reprise album How Does That Grab You? in 1966 and became ubiquitous after Kill Bill: Volume 1 used it over the opening credits in 2003.
Recorded 11 February 1966 at Gold Star Studios, Los Angeles, and released as a single by Imperial Records on 25 February 1966. It reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Bono wrote the song and produced Cher’s recording. Neither Cher nor Nancy Sinatra wrote it.

misattribution.truthLine: Cher recorded it first, in February 1966. Nancy Sinatra’s is a cover from the same year that a film made famous decades on.

context.heading: How a No. 2 hit lost its own song
lead: The usual shape of these stories is that a forgotten record got outsold by a famous one. This one is stranger: Cher’s original was not obscure at all. It reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 3 in the UK, and sold over a million copies. What overtook it was not a bigger hit but a better placement — Nancy Sinatra’s album track, sitting unremarked for decades, was picked by Quentin Tarantino for the opening credits of Kill Bill: Volume 1 in 2003.

That is the whole mechanism. Cher’s version was a radio hit for a season; Sinatra’s became a film’s signature, replayed for a generation that had no memory of the chart. Billy Strange’s spare tremolo guitar arrangement suits a revenge picture in a way that Sonny Bono’s bright 1966 production never could, so the cover reads as definitive to anyone who arrived through the cinema.
detailsBody: 11 February 1966 — Cher records the song at Gold Star Studios, Los Angeles. Sonny Bono, her husband, wrote it.
25 February 1966 — Imperial Records releases it as a single. It reaches No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 3 in the UK, and becomes Cher’s first million-selling single.
1966 — It appears on Cher’s album The Sonny Side of Chér.
May 1966 — Nancy Sinatra’s version appears on her Reprise album How Does That Grab You?, arranged by Billy Strange. It was not a Hot 100 hit.
1966 — Foreign-language versions top charts elsewhere: Sheila’s French recording reaches No. 1 in France in July, Dalida’s Italian version No. 1 in Italy.
2003 — Quentin Tarantino uses Sinatra’s recording over the opening credits of Kill Bill: Volume 1, and it becomes the version most listeners know.
2005 — UK duo Audio Bullys sample Sinatra’s recording on their electro house track “Shot You Down”; it reaches No. 3 in the UK and No. 20 in Australia.
context.pull: The original was a million-seller. The cover was a movie.
